source_text: οίσετε Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ ὑμῶν ἅλα.» Κατεπάττετο δὲ ἁλσὶν ἡ θυσία, τοῦ τύπου σημαίνοντος τὸ ἐμφρόνως χρῆναι καθιεροῦσθαι Θεῷ, καὶ οἱονεὶ ποιεῖσθαι νοστιμωτάτην αὐτῷ τὴν πρόσοδον. Οὐ γὰρ βρωθήσεται ἄρτος ἄνευ ἅλατος, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. «Ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς,» τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις προσπεφώνηκεν ὁ Χριστός. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ ἔφης. {ΚΥΡ.} Νόμοι μὲν οὖν οἴδε εἰσὶ, καθ' οὓς ἱερᾶσθαι πρέπει τοὺς ἡγιασμένους. Ὅτι δὲ τοὺς ἐξειλεγμένους, ἀρίστην ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς λαχόντας τὴν ψῆφον, ἀποφοιτᾷν ἀναγκαῖον καὶ βεβήλου συνουσίας, καὶ μερίμνης κοσμικῆς, ἐφ' ἧς ἂν γένοιτο καὶ τὸν εὖ βεβηκότα καταμεθύσκεσθαι νοῦν, καὶ μονονουχὶ κατασείεσθαι πρὸς ἐκτόπους ἡδονὰς, διασαφηνιεῖ λέγων ἐν τῷ Λευϊτικῷ· «Οἶνον καὶ σίκερα οὐ πίεσθε, σὺ καὶ οἱ υἱοί σου μετὰ σοῦ, ἡνίκα ἂν εἰσπορεύησθε εἰς τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ μαρτυρίου, ἢ προπορευομένων ὑμῶν εἰς τὸ θυσιαστήριον καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀποθάνητε· νόμιμον αἰώνιον εἰς τὰς γενεὰς ὑμῶν διαστεῖλαι ἀναμέσον τῶν ἁγίων καὶ τῶν βεβήλων, καὶ ἀναμέσον τῶν ἀκαθάρτων καὶ τῶν καθαρῶν. Καὶ συμβιβάσεις τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ ἅπαντα τὰ νόμιμα ἃ ἐλάλησε Κύριος πρὸς αὐτοὺς διὰ χειρὸς Μωσῆ.» Ἄθρει δὴ οὖν τὸ ἐγρηγορέναι δεῖν ἀναγκαῖον αὐτοῖς, καὶ θανάτου πρόξενον, τῷ νῷ κατεσκοτισμένῳ καὶ πεφροντισμένῃ καρδίᾳ, καὶ μέθην ἐχούσῃ κοσμικήν· μεθύουσι γὰρ ἄνευ οἴνου τινὲς, τὸ λειτουργίας ἅπτεσθαι τῆς ἱερᾶς. Οἴχεται γὰρ ἔσθ' ὅτε πρὸς τὸ ἀκαλλὲς ὁ νοῦς ὀρθοποδεῖν οὐκ ἔχων, καὶ διαπίπτει τὰ ἱερὰ, καὶ ἐν κόσμῳ μὲν οὐκέτι τὰ δρώμενα, διέῤῥιπται δὲ ὥσπερ τῆς εὐθείας ὁδοῦ· ὃ δὴ πεπονθότας, ἀνάγκη προσκρούειν Θεῷ, καὶ πικρὰς τῆς ῥᾳθυμίας ἀνατλῆναι δίκας. Ἐγρηγορέναι δὴ οὖν ἀναγκαῖον, μέθνη ἀποσειομένους, τὴν ἐκ μερίμνης κοσμικῆς. Τοῦτό τοι δρᾷν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Σωτὴρ ἀναπείθει, λέγων· «Προσέχετε μήποτε βαρυνθῶσιν αἱ καρδίαι ὑμῶν φροντίδι καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς.» Τίς δ' ἂν γένοιτο πρὸς ἡμῶν ὁ τῆς νήψεως τρόπος, ἢ πῶς ἀβέβηλοί τε καὶ καθαροὶ καὶ δίκης ἔξω μενοῦμεν, ὑπεσήμανεν εὐθύς. «Διάστειλαι γὰρ, φησὶν, ἀνὰ μέσον ἁγίου καὶ βεβήλου, καὶ καθαροῦ καὶ ἀκαθάρτου· καὶ συμβιβάσεις τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ ἅπαντα τὰ νόμιμα, ἃ ἐλάλησε Κύριος ἐν χειρὶ Μωσῆ.» Τοῦτο δέ ἐστιν ἐναργῶς ἐκεῖνο εἰπεῖν, ὅτι προσήκει τοὺς ἱερέας τὸ μεθύειν ἀποσειομένους, ἀποφοιτᾷν ἀνδρῶν οὐχ ἁγίων, βεβήλων δὲ καὶ ἀκαθάρτων. Δρῴη δ' ἂν, οἶμαι, τὶς αὐτὸ καὶ μάλα ῥᾳδίως, ἀβέβηλός τε ὑπάρχων καὶ καθαρός· «Πᾶν γὰρ ζῶον, φησὶν, ἀγαπᾷ τὸ ὅμοιον αὐτῷ, καὶ τῷ ὁμοίῳ αὐτοῦ προσκολληθήσεται ἀνήρ.» Καὶ πρός γε δὴ τούτῳ, σοφοὺς εἶναι προσήκει καὶ διδακτικούς· ὁ γάρ τοι τῆς λογικῆς ἀγέλης προσεγκείμενος, νηφάλιος ἔστω καὶ διδακτικός. Εὖ γε δὴ σφόδρα τὸ, Συμβιβάσεις, φησὶ, τοῦτ' ἔστι, σαφηνιεῖς, ὡς ἰσχύσαι συνιδεῖν τοὺς ἀκροωμένους, ὡς ἔστι παιδαγωγὸς ὁ νόμος, καὶ λαλεῖ τὸ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον· δυσέφικτον γὰρ οὐδέν. ἢ συμβιβασμοῦ δεόμενον, εἰ μὴ νοοῖτο πνευματικῶς· κομιδῇ γὰρ ἁπλοῦς καὶ τῶν ἀσαφείας κατασκιασμάτων ὁ τῆς ἱστορίας ἀπήλλακται λόγος.
pass_a_gloss: [Lev 2:13 end] '...you shall bring (προσοίσετε) to Lord your God salt (ἅλα).' The sacrifice was sprinkled (κατεπάττετο) with salts, the type signifying (τύπος σημαίνει) that it must be consecrated (καθιεροῦσθαι) to God wisely/with understanding (ἐμφρόνως), and as it were make the approach/offering (πρόσοδος) most savoury (νοστιμωτάτην) to Him. For bread will not be eaten without salt, according to what is written. 'You are the salt of the earth,' Christ addressed (προσπεφώνηκεν) to the holy apostles. PALL.: You spoke well. CYR.: These then are laws by which it befits the sanctified (ἡγιασμένους) to act as priests (ἱερᾶσθαι). That those chosen out (ἐξειλεγμένους), having obtained the best vote (ψῆφος) upon themselves, must withdraw (ἀποφοιτᾶν) from profane company (βεβήλου συνουσίας) and worldly care (μερίμνης κοσμικῆς), upon which even the well-set mind (εὖ βεβηκότα νοῦν) might become drunk (καταμεθύσκεσθαι) and all but (μονονουχί) be shaken down toward out-of-place pleasures (ἐκτόπους ἡδονάς), he will make clear saying in Leviticus: [Lev 10:9-11] 'Wine and sikera you shall not drink, you and your sons with you, whenever you go into the tent of witness, or as you go forward to the altar, and you shall not die; perpetual statute (νόμιμον αἰώνιον) into your generations, to distinguish (διαστεῖλαι) between holy and profane (βεβήλων), and between unclean and clean. And you shall instruct (συμβιβάσεις) the sons of Israel all the statutes which the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses.' Observe then that it is necessary for them to be awake (ἐγρηγορέναι), and that it is a bringer of death (θανάτου πρόξενον) to touch the sacred liturgy with the mind darkened and a heart full of cares (πεφροντισμένῃ) and having worldly drunkenness (μέθην κοσμικήν) — for some are drunk without wine. For at times the mind goes off toward the unseemly (ἀκαλλές), not able to walk upright (ὀρθοποδεῖν), and the sacred things fall apart (διαπίπτει), and the rites (δρώμενα) are no longer in order (ἐν κόσμῳ), but are flung aside as it were from the straight road; having suffered which, they must strike against (προσκρούειν) God and endure bitter penalties (δίκας) of their carelessness (ῥᾳθυμίας). So it is necessary to be awake, shaking off (ἀποσειομένους) the drunkenness from worldly care. This the Saviour Himself urges, saying: 'Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down (βαρυνθῶσιν) with anxiety (φροντίδι) and cares of life (μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς).' What would be our manner of sobriety (νήψεως), or how we shall remain unprofaned and clean and outside of penalty, he indicated at once: 'Distinguish between holy and profane, clean and unclean; and you shall instruct the sons of Israel all the statutes which the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses.' This is plainly to say that the priests, shaking off drunkenness, should withdraw from men not holy but profane and unclean. One would do it, I think, very easily, being himself unprofaned and clean: 'For every living creature loves its like, and a man will cling (προσκολληθήσεται) to his like.' And in addition to this they must be wise and apt to teach (διδακτικούς); for the one set over (προσεγκείμενος) the rational flock (λογικῆς ἀγέλης) must be sober (νηφάλιος) and apt to teach. Very well indeed is 'You shall instruct' (συμβιβάσεις), that is, 'you shall make clear' (σαφηνιεῖς), so that the hearers can perceive that the law is a tutor (παιδαγωγός) and speaks the mystery of Christ. For nothing is hard to reach (δυσέφικτον) or in need of instruction (συμβιβασμοῦ), unless it is understood spiritually (πνευματικῶς); for the account of the history (ὁ τῆς ἱστορίας λόγος) is entirely simple and freed from the shadows of obscurity (ἀσαφείας κατασκιασμάτων).
pass_b_english: Cyril: ‘…you shall offer salt to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 2:13). The sacrifice was sprinkled with salt, the type signifying that one must be consecrated to God with understanding, and make one’s approach to him, as it were, most savoury. For bread will not be eaten without salt, as it is written (Job 6:6). Christ said to the holy apostles: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13).

Cyril: These, then, are the laws by which those who have been sanctified ought to serve as priests. But those who have been chosen, on whom the best verdict has fallen, must keep away both from profane company and from worldly care. Through such care even a steady mind may become drunk, and all but be toppled into improper pleasures. He makes this clear when he says in Leviticus: ‘You shall not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, whenever you go into the tent of witness or approach the altar, so that you do not die. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, to distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the unclean and the clean. And you shall teach the sons of Israel all the statutes that the Lord spoke to them by the hand of Moses’ (Leviticus 10:9–11).

See, then, that they must keep awake. To handle the sacred liturgy with a darkened mind, and with an anxious heart that is drunk with worldly things, brings death; for some are drunk without wine. For at times the mind, unable to walk upright, slips away toward what is unseemly; the sacred things fall into disarray, and what is performed is no longer in good order but is thrown, as it were, off the straight road. Those who suffer this cannot help but offend God and endure bitter penalties for their carelessness. So one must keep awake and shake off the drunkenness that comes from worldly care. The Savior himself also urges this when he says: ‘Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by anxiety and the cares of this life’ (Luke 21:34).

What our way of sobriety would be, and how we shall remain unprofaned and clean and free of punishment, he indicated at once. For ‘distinguish,’ He says, ‘between holy and profane, and between clean and unclean; and you shall teach the sons of Israel all the statutes that the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses’ (Leviticus 10:10–11). This plainly means that the priests, having shaken off drunkenness, ought to keep away from men who are not holy but profane and unclean. And I think a man would do this very easily if he is himself unprofaned and clean; for ‘every living creature,’ it says, ‘loves its like, and a man will cling to one like himself’ (Sirach 13:15–16).

Besides this, they ought to be wise and able to teach; for whoever has charge of the rational flock must be sober and able to teach (1 Timothy 3:2). He puts it very well when he says, ‘You shall teach,’ that is, ‘You shall make plain,’ so that the hearers may be able to see that the law is a tutor (Galatians 3:24) and speaks the mystery of Christ. For nothing in it is hard to grasp or needs teaching, unless it is understood spiritually; for the historical account is entirely simple and free of the shadows of obscurity.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril De adoratione Book 12 exists. Translated fresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the earlier English of this book was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

Section opens mid-quotation: the end of Leviticus 2:13 LXX ('upon every gift of yours you shall offer salt to the Lord your God'), begun at the close of section 30. 'Bread will not be eaten without salt' is Job 6:6 LXX, which asks it as a question; Cyril cites it as a statement. The old English wrongly placed Sirach 13:15 beside Matthew 5:13, Leviticus 2:13 beside the Leviticus 10 quotation, Matthew 5:13 beside Luke 21:34, and Galatians 3:24 beside Leviticus 10:10; all corrected here. Leviticus 10:9–11 follows the LXX closely (σικερα = strong drink; συμβιβάσεις = 'you shall teach'). Cyril's form of Luke 21:34 has 'anxiety and cares of this life' (φροντίδι καὶ μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς) in place of the standard 'dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life'. Sirach 13:15–16 joins two LXX verses. 'Sober and apt to teach' for one over the flock is a clear allusion to 1 Timothy 3:2 (νηφάλιον ... διδακτικόν). 'The law is a tutor' alludes to Galatians 3:24 (παιδαγωγός). 'Some are drunk without wine' may echo Isaiah 29:9 or 51:21 LXX, but the wording is not close enough; left uncited. OCR: μέθνη read as μέθην. In the last sentence I punctuate δυσέφικτον γὰρ οὐδὲν ἢ συμβιβασμοῦ δεόμενον as one clause (the printed full stop before ἢ looks like an error). 'Ἐν κόσμῳ' is rendered 'in good order'. The sentence beginning Ἄθρει is compressed in the Greek; I take θανάτου πρόξενον as predicate of τὸ λειτουργίας ἅπτεσθαι τῆς ἱερᾶς, with 'some are drunk without wine' as a parenthesis.

Removed added 'also'; καὶ ... καὶ rendered 'both ... and'
'Under such care ... stands firm ... shaken loose toward strange pleasures' -> 'Through such care even a steady mind ... toppled into improper pleasures' (ἐκτόπους, potential ἂν kept as 'may')
Leviticus 10:9 'come up to the altar' -> 'approach the altar'
'To lay hands on' (reads as seizing/ordaining) -> 'To handle the sacred liturgy'; πεφροντισμένῃ καρδίᾳ -> 'an anxious heart'
Restored omitted γάρ ('For at times the mind'); removed added 'then'; διέρριπται -> 'thrown'
Impersonal Ἐγρηγορέναι ἀναγκαῖον -> 'one must' (not 'they'); removed added 'us', restored καὶ ('also urges this')
Luke 21:34 'Take heed, lest' (archaic) -> 'Take care that your hearts are not weighed down'
Τίς ἂν γένοιτο: 'should be' -> 'would be'; restored γάρ before Leviticus 10:10 quotation
διδακτικούς / διδακτικός rendered 'able to teach' both times; 'very well does He say' -> 'He puts it very well'
Restored second γάρ; 'the account of the history is quite simple' -> 'the historical account is entirely simple' (κομιδῇ)
